What should happen when someone knowingly makes a false accusation about a serious crime like assault? This isn't about dismissing real victims, because real victims deserve Protection. But false accusations can destroy innocent lives. Brian Banks served over five years in prison before his accuser admitted she lied and she faced no prison time. And in that same case, whenetta Gibson was later ordered to pay about $2.6 million. But reports showed she didn't have the money. And even if she did, there's not enough money in the world to give someone those years back. Gary Dodson spent years behind bars before his accuser, Kathleen Crowell Webb, recanted exposing the false claim. Anthony Broadwater lost over 16 years of his life after a wrongful accusation and was only cleared decades later. And while he later received a settlement, there's not enough money in the world to restore that lost time, reputation, and peace. These situations show a real gap in accountability, because when someone lies about a crime this serious, the consequences for the accused don't just disappear. When the truth comes out, years are lost that can never be returned. At the same time, real victims already struggle to come forward, which is why this conversation has to stay balanced. But fairness goes both ways. In my opinion, if someone knowingly makes a false accusation that leads to an innocent person serving time, they should serve that same amount of time. And if no time was served, there should still Be a real consequence. At least one year in prison for false statements. Justice can't be one sided. Accountability has to match the damage caused.

Hey, have you ever wondered why people like Elon Musk, Bill Gates, Jeff Bezos and Mark Zuckerberg, the billionaires, the so called 1%, often seem to pay less in taxes than everyday working people? It feels backwards. You work, you get taxed right out of your paycheck, while some of the richest people report relatively low taxable income. So what happened? A major part of that answer goes back to Ronald Reagan and the shift in economic policy during the 1980s. Before Reagan, under leaders like Jimmy Carter, the top federal tax rate was as high as 70%, meaning the wealthiest Americans were taxed heavily on income. Reagan introduced supply side economics, which argued that cutting taxes, especially for businesses and high earners, would boost investment and grow the economy. In 1981, he cut the top tax rate to 50%, and by 1986 it dropped to 28%, one of the biggest reductions in U S. History. But the real shift was not just lower rates, it was how money is taxed. Most working people earn wages, which are taxed immediately. Billionaires build wealth through assets like stocks and investments, and those gains are not taxed unless they are sold. So when their wealth grows by billions, it is often considered unrealized gains, meaning no sale, no tax. On top of that, many use legal strategies like borrowing against their assets, giving them access to cash without triggering income taxes. Reagan did not create today's system alone, but his policies marked a turning Point lowering taxes at the top and reshaping how wealth is treated. Over time, this helped create a system where income from work is taxed more consistently than wealth from investments. So when people say billionaires pay less taxes, it is not always about breaking rules. It is about how the system is designed. And that design started shifting decades ago.

The faces you see in this video are some of the thousands of children listed on Missing kids.org. I'm here to bring awareness to an issue many people rarely stop to think about. Years ago, missing children were printed on milk cartons across the country so families would see their faces at breakfast tables everyday. The program ended in the 1990s because it was inconsistent, expensive, and sometimes displayed cases that were already solved by the time cartons reached stores. Today, awareness mostly relies on digital tools like Amber Alert sent to phones and highway signs, online databases like Missing kids dot org, and social media posts shared by law enforcement and organisations. Many people still believe families must wait 24 hours before reporting a child missing. That is not true. There is no law requiring a waiting period. A missing child can and should be reported immediately. The longer authorities wait to begin searching, the harder it becomes to trace where the child went, identify witnesses, or recover useful surveillance footage. Every year in the United States, thousands of children are reported missing, and the first few hours are the most critical. Another problem is inconsistency in how cases are handled. Resources, urgency, and coordination can vary depending on the department and where the disappearance happens. Smaller agencies may not have specialised units for missing children, and communication across jurisdictions can slow the process. Families often feel they must push for their child's case to receive attention. At the same Time. The United States has technology capable of locating people quickly. Facial recognition can identify suspects within minutes using public cameras. Automated license plate readers track vehicles across cities and highways, and national databases connect agencies to locate fugitives. These systems show how fast identification and tracking can work. Yet families often question why the same level of urgency is not always used when a child disappears. Looking through the list, another pattern appears. Many of the missing children are girls. Experts say girls are statistically more likely to be targeted for certain forms of exploitation and trafficking, which may contribute to these numbers. If a child goes missing, act immediately. Contact local law enforcement right away. You can also contact the National Centre for missing and Exploited Children at 18HUNDRED THE lost 1 808 4 3 5 6 7 8. The line is available 24 hours a day to help start the search and distribute information nationwide. Although digital tools are the future, sometimes nothing spreads awareness like the simple idea that once worked putting missing children's faces on milk cartons for families everywhere to see.

The people you are seeing were victims of the Jonestown Massacre, one of the most tragic events in modern history. In November 1978, more than 900 people died in the remote settlement of Jonestown in Guyana. They were followers of Jim Jones, the leader of the People's Temple. Many of the victims were African American men, women, and children who had joined the People's Temple believing it stood for Equality, community, and Protection from racism during a difficult time in the United States. Jim Jones convinced hundreds of people to move to Jonestown with promises of a better life and a safe, unified community. Instead, the settlement became isolated and tightly controlled. Followers were cut off from the outside world and pressured to obey Jones without question. On November 18th, 1978, after increasing outside scrutiny, Jones ordered what he called revolutionary suicide. A large container of flavoured drink mix was poisoned and members were coerced or forced to drink it. Children were given the poison by adults under Jones's orders. The victims of Jonestown were not simply participants in a strange event. Many were people searching for hope, safety, and belonging. Their lives were taken through manipulation, fear, and the abuse of trust by a leader who held complete control over the community. Their story remains a powerful reminder of how dangerous unchecked power and manipulation can become.

Did you know there are about 15 million vacant homes in the U. S? It sounds shocking, but there's an important detail people miss. The U S. Census Bureau shows that the largest share of vacant homes are seasonal, vacation or second properties, not houses just sitting there waiting for families. Once you remove those, the picture changes. We're left with year round vacant homes, and even then only a tiny portion are actually on the market at a given time. The census reported a homeowner vacancy rate of about 1.2%. That's the slice of homes truly available for sale in the homeowner inventory. That's extremely tight supply. So why are homes still empty while people struggle to buy? Many are tied up in probate, legal disputes or need major repairs. Others are held off the market by owners or investors waiting for better prices. Some sellers refuse to lower prices after years of rising home values and today's higher mortgage rates make buyers back off. There's also rate lock in where owners with ultra low pandemic mortgage rates don't wanna sell and take on a higher one. And why not just sell cheap? Because for many owners, cheap means losing money after maintenance, taxes or renovations. It can hurt neighbourhood property values and investors often prefer to wait rather than accept a loss. Housing is treated like an asset first, shelter second. Japan faces a similar but even larger issue. The country had around 9 million vacant homes, about 13.8% of Housing as of 2023, according to Japan's Ministry of Internal Affairs and communications. But unlike the U S, Japan has expanded IKEA banks, local government programs listing empty homes, sometimes for extremely low prices, while offering tax breaks and renovation subsidies to get people to move in and restore them. Could the U S. Do something similar? Financially, large scale housing programs are possible, but the challenge here is legal and structural. Property rights are strong, housing policy is split across thousands of local governments, and many vacant homes aren't publicly owned. Turning them into affordable housing would require incentives, tax changes, rehabilitation, funding, and coordination on a scale the U S. Rarely achieves. Still, with homelessness and affordability crisis growing, the bigger question isn't whether America can afford to act, it's whether it chooses to treat housing as essential infrastructure instead of just an investment.

Ever wonder why your favourite billionaires aren't taxed like you and me? Yeah, the people who somehow pay a lower effective tax rate than a teacher or a nurse, yet own jets, yachts, and five houses. And no, it's not because they're hiding piles of cash in a vault somewhere. Here's the part most people miss. Billionaires don't actually have most of their money in cash. Their wealth lives in assets. Stocks, companies, real estate. Things that grow in value but aren't taxed until they're sold. And since our tax system taxes income you receive, not wealth you hold, they can legally avoid triggering taxes for years, sometimes decades. So I know what you're wondering. If they don't have cash, how are they affording all these luxuries? Simple. They don't spend their wealth, they borrow against it. When you own billions in assets, banks will happily loan you millions at extremely low interest, using those assets as collateral. That loan money isn't considered income, so it's not taxed. That's what pays for the mansions, private jets, yachts, and luxury lifestyles. Perfectly legal, perfectly normal at that level. Meanwhile, if you and I want money, we have to work for it, get paid, and get taxed immediately. There's no borrowing against our future paycheck to live tax free. That's the difference. Wealth creates leverage, and leverage creates access to money without triggering taxes. And here's where it really gets interesting. Because they rarely sell those assets, they avoid capital gains taxes. Altogether, then when they die, the law allows something called a stepped up basis, which resets the value of those assets to current market prices. Translation their heirs can sell with little or no tax on decades of growth. The system quietly wipes the slate clean. This isn't a conspiracy. It's not illegal, it's not secret. It's written into the tax code and openly used by the ultra wealthy. The reason it feels unfair is because it kind of is. The system was designed around income, not extreme asset based wealth. And the ultra rich know exactly how to play within those rules. So when people ask why don't we just tax billionaires? The real answer isn't that we can't. It's that the way their money works is completely different from how yours does. And until that changes, they'll keep living lavishly, borrowing tax free and paying less, while the rest of us get taxed the moment our paycheck hits.

Every day in the United States, the lottery quietly moves more money than most people realise. On average, Americans spend roughly $300 million a day on lottery tickets. That comes out to well over $100 billion a year. It is one of the most consistent cash flows in the country. Not because the odds are good, but because hope is powerful, especially when people feel stuck, stressed, or financially desperate. The lottery thrives in moments of pressure when wages lag, debt rises, and the future feels uncertain. A few dollars for a ticket feels like relief. It feels like a shortcut. But mathematically, the lottery is designed so that the vast majority of players lose over and over again. The odds of winning a major Powerball Jackpot are about 1 in 292 million. That is not a strategy that is a long shot sold as a dream. When people do win, the picture is very different from what most imagine. The average large Jackpot winner is not a young person starting life. Studies and surveys of winners consistently place the average age in the early to mid 50s. Many winners have already lived most of their working lives. That alone changes how the money actually impacts their future. Certain states appear to win more, but that perception is driven by population and ticket sales, not luck. States like California, Florida, New York, Texas, and historically, Indiana show up often simply because they sell more tickets. More tickets means more winners. There is no magic state No lucky region, just volume. The part rarely advertised is what happens after the cameras leave. While the viral claim that most winners go broke is exaggerated, the reality is still uncomfortable. A significant minority of big winners eventually face serious financial trouble. Some declare bankruptcy. Others lose relationships, privacy, or peace of mind. The money exposes weaknesses that were already there and adds pressure that most people are not trained to handle. There are infamous stories that illustrate the dark side. Billy Bob Harold junior, a Texas winner, gave generously to family, friends and strangers until the money and the pressure collapsed his life. Abraham Shakespeare won millions in Florida and was later murdered by someone who manipulated and exploited him. These are extreme cases, but they are real and they reveal a pattern. Sudden money attracts sudden problems. Many winners do fine. Some improve their quality of life, help their families responsibly, and live more comfortably without imploding. The difference is not luck. It is structure, pacing and restraint. This is where the choice between lump sum and increments, also called an annuity, becomes critical. The advertised Jackpot is almost always the annuity value paid out over 20 to 30 years. The lump sum is much smaller upfront. On top of that, a lump sum creates a massive tax hit in a single year. Federal withholding A loan starts at 24%, but top winners often owe closer to 37% federally plus state taxes depending on where they live. What looks like hundreds of millions on paper can shrink dramatically before it ever reaches a bank account. Incremental payments spread the money and the taxes over decades. They create enforced discipline. You cannot spend money you have not received yet. That pacing protects winners from reckless early decisions, bad investments, predatory advisors, and emotional spending fueled by shock and pressure. Increments turn one win into long term income, sometimes for life. Instead of a single explosive moment, people still choose the lump sum, and most winners do. They want control. They distrust long term payouts. They believe they can invest better themselves. They want to pay everything off immediately. They are surrounded by people urging them to act fast. The problem is that speed is what destroys them. Too much money too quickly, with no buffer for mistakes. Responsible gambling means understanding that the lottery is entertainment, not a financial plan. If someone plays, it should be with strict limits, never with money needed for bills, and never as a response to desperation. Chasing losses is how people quietly fall into financial holes. If someone ever does win, the steps matter more than the Celebration. The ticket should be signed immediately and secured. The win should not be announced publicly without legal advice. A lawyer should come first to handle privacy and claim structure. A tax professional should follow immediately. Spending should pause. Family help should be structured, not emotional, and the default choice should be increments, not lump Sum the lottery has a good side. It funds programs. It creates rare opportunities. It can change lives for the better. But it also has an ugly side. Built on desperation, unrealistic expectations, and financial ignorance. The system always wins. A few people get lucky, and those who survive the win are almost always the ones who slow the money down. If you ever win, do not rush. Take the increments. Let time work for you instead of against you. Decades of stability. Beat one fast check that disappears. And if you never win, remember this. The safest way to beat the lottery is not to believe it will save you.

Lucas changed the history of brain cancer and exposed a broken system. For decades, brain cancer, especially rare childhood forms like diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma, D I P G, has been one of the most devastating diagnoses in medicine. Children were routinely told they had months to live, not because doctors didn't care, but because science had no effective treatments and the system failed to prioritise these rare cases. In the United States, cancer treatment is a massive industry. Cancer drugs generate tens of billions of dollars every year, with projections reaching hundreds of billions globally in the coming decade. However, brain cancers represent only a small fraction of that revenue, roughly a few billion dollars annually, and rare pediatric brain cancers like D I P G. Account for only a tiny slice of that already small portion. Because these cancers affect relatively few patients and are biologically complex, they historically received less research funding, fewer drug trials, and slower progress. That context matters. At age 6, Lucas, a Belgian child, was diagnosed with D I P G, a cancer where most children do not survive a year. His family was told to prepare for the worst. Instead of accepting that fate, they travelled to France, where Lucas was enrolled in the Biomed clinical trial at the Gustave Roussy Cancer Centre. What happened next changed medical history. Lucas responded dramatically to the drug everolimus, not because it was a guaranteed cure, but because his tumor carried an extremely rare genetic mutation, That made it uniquely vulnerable. Over time, M R I. Scans showed something doctors had never seen before. The tumor completely disappeared. Today, Lucas is 13 years old, cancer free, living a normal life and no longer on treatment. He is the first known child in the world to be cured of this form of brain cancer. This breakthrough did not come from profit driven medicine. It came from public research, international collaboration, long term trials, and scientists willing to study children even when success wasn't guaranteed. Lucas's case is now guiding new research that could one day help other children. But doctors are clear. Turning this discovery into a widely available treatment will still take 10, 15 years. Lucas's story proves something important. Not that cures were hidden, not that doctors refused to help, but that rare childhood cancers were underserved in a system driven by scale, speed, and return on investment. Lucas didn't just survive. He rewrote what was thought possible. And his life stands as both a victory and a reminder that when science, funding, and compassion finally align, even the most incurable cancers can fall.

Why do March natural gas futures cover April, but April doesn't cover March? It's more intuitive than you think. Most beginner traders think that hedging works both ways for natural gas, but it doesn't. The difference comes down to seasonal demand risk. March is the tail end of winter and April is a shoulder month. In March, heating demand is still high, but in April, heating demand drops off. A cold snap in April is less likely and less severe. This is what makes March riskier than April. March trades at a premium to April. This is what's known as backwardation. That premium reflects the winter tail risk. When you buy March, you're buying insurance against a late season cold snap. But when you're buying April, you're not buying that insurance. You're exposed to March spikes. That's why March covers April, but April doesn't cover March. The March April spread is notorious in the industry. They call it the widowmaker because of how volatile it is. As winter progresses, the spread can narrow or flip, but the risk of a sudden severe cold still remains higher in March than in April. This makes March the robust insurance policy against volatility. This is how professionals think about energy hedging. They understand seasonal risk and how real life events can affect pricing. This equation moves billions of dollars in quant trading every single day. It's called the Kelly criterion. It's a formula from probability theory that helps you size your bets to maximize long term growth. In this formula, P is your probability of winning, Q is the opposite of P or your probability of losing, and B is how much you stand to gain per dollar risked. The result, F Star is the optimal bet size. You estimate P&B from your models and past trades, and you calculate how much to put on each trade. For example, if you have a 60% chance at even odds, then the Kelly fraction is 20%. Betting that amount can outperform more conservative bets like 5% or 10% over a longer period of time. This is why Kelly sizing is especially popular for option strategies where probability and payoff are fairly well defined. In the real world, probabilities are noisy and markets are constantly changing. Going full Kelly can produce huge drawdowns. Most professional traders use fractional Kelly, typically 20 to 25% of the calculated amount. This cushions against estimation errors and volatility.
